groups.title: Moving to Banford City
groups.instruction: Complete the notes. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

transcript.text: Hello, Linda speaking.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: Oh hi, Linda.
transcript.speaker: MATT

transcript.text: This is Matt Brooks.
transcript.speaker: MATT

transcript.text: Alex White gave me your number.
transcript.speaker: MATT

transcript.text: He said you’d be able to give me some advice about moving to Banford.
transcript.speaker: MATT

transcript.text: Yes, Alex did mention you.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: How can I help?
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: Well, first of all – which area to live in?
transcript.speaker: MATT

transcript.text: Well, I live in Dalton, which is a really nice suburb – not too expensive, and there’s a nice park.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: Sounds good.
transcript.speaker: MATT

transcript.text: Do you know how much it would be to rent a two bedroom flat there?
transcript.speaker: MATT

transcript.text: Yeah, you should be able to get something reasonable for 850 pounds per month.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: That’s what people typically pay.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: You certainly wouldn’t want to pay more than 900 pounds.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: That doesn’t include bills or anything.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: No.
transcript.speaker: MATT

transcript.text: That sound alright.
transcript.speaker: MATT

transcript.text: I’ll definitely have a look there.
transcript.speaker: MATT

transcript.text: Are the transport links easy from where you live?
transcript.speaker: MATT

transcript.text: Well, I’m very lucky.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: I work in the city centre so I don’t have to use public transport.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: I go by bike.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: Oh, I wish I could do that.
transcript.speaker: MATT

transcript.text: Is it safe to cycle around the city?
transcript.speaker: MATT

transcript.text: Yes, it’s fine.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: And it keeps me fit.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: Anyway, driving to work in the city centre would be a nightmare because there’s hardly any parking.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: And the traffic during the rush hour can be bad.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: I’d be working from home but I’d have to go to London one or two days a week.
transcript.speaker: MATT

transcript.text: Oh, that’s perfect.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: Getting to London is no problem.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: There’s a fast train every 30 minutes which only takes 45 minutes.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: That’s good.
transcript.speaker: MATT

transcript.text: Yeah, the train service isn’t bad during the week.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: And they run quite late at night.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: It’s weekends that are a problem.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: They’re always doing engineering work and you have to take a bus to Hadham and pick up the train there, which is really slow.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: But other than that, Banford’s a great place to live.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: I’ve never been happier.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: There are some nice restaurants in the city centre and a brand new cinema which has only been open a couple of months.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: There’s a good arts centre too.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: Sounds like Banford’s got it all.
transcript.speaker: MATT

transcript.text: Yes!
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: We’re really lucky.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: There are lots of really good aspects to living here.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: The schools are good and the hospital here is one of the best in the country.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: Everyone I know who’s been there’s had a positive experience.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: Oh, I can give you the name of my dentist too in Bridge Street, if you’re interested.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: I’ve been going to him for years and I’ve never had any problems.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: Oh, OK.
transcript.speaker: MATT

transcript.text: Thanks!
transcript.speaker: MATT

transcript.text: I’ll find his number and send it to you.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: Thanks, that would be really helpful.
transcript.speaker: MATT

transcript.text: Are you planning to visit Banford soon?
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: MATT

transcript.text: My wife and I are both coming next week.
transcript.speaker: MATT

transcript.text: We want to make some appointments with estate agents.
transcript.speaker: MATT

transcript.text: I could meet you if you like and show you around.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: Are you sure?
transcript.speaker: MATT

transcript.text: We’d really appreciate that.
transcript.speaker: MATT

transcript.text: Either a Tuesday or Thursday is good for me, after 5.30.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: Thursday’s preferable – Tuesday I need to get home before 6 pm.
transcript.speaker: MATT

transcript.text: Okay great.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: Let me know which train your catching and I’ll meet you in the cafe outside.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: You can’t miss it.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: It’s opposite the station and next to the museum.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: Brilliant.
transcript.speaker: MATT

transcript.text: I’ll text you next week then.
transcript.speaker: MATT

transcript.text: Thanks so much for all the advice.
transcript.speaker: MATT

transcript.text: No problem.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

transcript.text: I’ll see you next week.
transcript.speaker: LINDA

groups.instruction: Choose TWO letters, A–E. Answers may be given in either order.

transcript.text: So if you are one of those people who hasn’t found the perfect physical activity yet, here are some things to think about which might help you make the right decision for you.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The first question to ask yourself is whether you would enjoy training in a gym.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Many people are put off by the idea of having to fit a visit to the gym into their busy day.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: You often have to go very early or late as some gyms can get very crowded but with regular training you’ll see a big difference in a relatively short space of time.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Running has become incredibly popular in recent years.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: That’s probably got a lot to do with the fact that it’s a very accessible form of exercise that anyone can run even if you could only run a few meters to begin with.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: But make sure you get the right shoes.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: It’s worth investing in a high quality pair and they don’t come cheap.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Another great thing about running is that you can do it at any time of day or night.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The only thing that may stop you is snow and ice.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Swimming is another really good way to build fitness.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: What attracts many people is that you can swim in an indoor pool at any time of year.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: On the other hand, it can be quite boring or solitary.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: It’s hard to chat to people while you’re swimming lengths.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Cycling has become almost as popular as running in recent years.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: That’s probably because as well as improving their fitness many people say being out in the fresh air in a park or in the countryside can be fun, provided the conditions are right of course.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Only fanatics go out in the wind and rain.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Yoga is a good choice for those of you looking for exercise, which focuses on developing both a healthy mind and body.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: It’s a good way of building strength and with the right instructor there’s less chance of hurting yourself than with other more active sports.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: But don’t expect to find it easy.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: It can be surprisingly challenging, especially for people who aren’t very flexible.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Getting a personal trainer is a good way to start your fitness program.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Obviously there can be significant costs involved.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: But if you’ve got someone there to encourage you and help you achieve your goals, you’re less likely to give up.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Make sure you get someone with a recognised qualification though.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Or you could do yourself permanent damage.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Whatever you do, don’t join a gym unless you’re sure you’ll make good use of it.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: So many people waste lots of money by signing up for membership and then hardly ever go.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: What happens to their good intentions?
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: I don’t think people suddenly stop caring about improving their fitness or decide they have more important things to do.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: I think people lose interest when they don’t think they’re making enough progress. That’s when they give up hope and stop believing they’ll ever achieve their goals. Also, what people sometimes don’t realize when they start is that it takes a lot of determination and hard work to keep training week after week, and lots of people don’t have that kind of commitment.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: One thing you can do to help yourself is to set manageable goals, be realistic and don’t push yourself too far. Some people advise writing goals down but I think it’s better to have a flexible approach. Give yourself a really nice treat every time you reach one of your goals and don’t get too upset if you experience setbacks.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: It’s a journey.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: There are bound to be difficulties along the way.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

groups.title: Project on using natural dyes to colour fabrics

options.text: It is unsuitable for some fabrics.

parts.context: Project on using natural dyes to colour fabrics

transcript.text: OK, Jim.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: You wanted to see me about your textile design project.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: That’s right.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: I’ve been looking at how a range of natural dyes can be used to colour fabrics like cotton and wool.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: Why did you choose that topic?
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Well, I got a lot of useful ideas from the museum, you know, at that exhibition of textiles.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: But I’ve always been interested in anything to do with colour.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: Years ago, I went to a carpet shop with my parents when we were on holiday in Turkey, and I remember all the amazing colours.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: They might not all have been natural dyes.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Maybe not, but for the project I decided to follow it up.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: And I found a great book about a botanic garden in California that specialises in plants used for dyes.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: So, in your project, you had to include a practical investigation.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Yeah.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: At first I couldn’t decide on my variables.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: I was going to just look at one type of fibre for example, like cotton …
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: … and see how different types of dyes affected it?
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: Then I decided to include others as well, so I looked at cotton and wool and nylon.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: With just one type of dye?
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Various types, including some that weren’t natural, for comparison.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: So, I did the experiments last week.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: I used some ready-made natural dyes.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: I found a website which supplied them, they came in just a few days, but I also made some of my own.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: That must have taken quite a bit of time.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Yes, I’d thought it’d just be a matter of a teaspoon or so of dye, and actually that wasn’t the case at all.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: Like I was using one vegetable, beetroot, for a red dye, and I had to chop up a whole pile of it.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: So it all took longer than I’d expected.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: One possibility is to use food colourings.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: I did use one.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: That was a yellow dye, an artificial one.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: Tartrazine?
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Yeah.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: I used it on cotton first.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: It came out a great colour, but when I rinsed the material, the colour just washed away.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: I’d been going to try it out on nylon, but I abandoned that idea.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: Were you worried about health issues?
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: I’d thought if it’s a legal food colouring, it must be safe.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: Well, it can occasionally cause allergic reactions, I believe.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: So what natural dyes did you look at?
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Well, one was turmeric.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: The colour’s great, it’s a really strong yellow.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: It’s generally used in dishes like curry.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: It’s meant to be quite good for your health when eaten, but you might find it’s not permanent when it’s used as a dye – a few washes, and it’s gone.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: I used beetroot as a dye for wool.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: When I chop up beetroot to eat I always end up with bright red hands, but the wool ended up just a sort of watery cream shade.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: Disappointing.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: There’s a natural dye called Tyrian purple.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Have you heard of that?
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: It comes from a shellfish, and it was worn in ancient times but only by important people as it was so rare.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: I didn’t use it.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: It fell out of use centuries ago, though one researcher managed to get hold of some recently.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: But that shade of purple can be produced by chemical dyes nowadays.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Did you use any black dyes?
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Logwood.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: That was quite complicated.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: I had to prepare the fabric so the dye would take.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: I hope you were careful to wear gloves.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: I know the danger with that dye.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: Good.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: It can be extremely dangerous if it’s ingested.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Now, presumably you had a look at an insect-based dye?
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Like cochineal, for example?
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: I didn’t actually make that, I didn’t have time to start crushing up insects to get the red colour and anyway they’re not available here, but I managed to get the dye quite easily from a website.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: But it cost a fortune.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: I can see why it’s generally just used in cooking, and in small quantities.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: Yes, it’s very effective, but that’s precisely why it’s not used as a dye.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: I also read about using metal oxide.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: Apparently you can allow iron to rust while it’s in contact with the fabric, and that colours it.
transcript.speaker: JIM

transcript.text: Yes, that works well for dyeing cotton.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: But you have to be careful as the metal can actually affect the fabric and so you can’t expect to get a lot of wear out of fabrics treated in this way.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: And the colours are quite subtle, not everyone likes them.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: Anyway, it looks as if you’ve done a lot of work …
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

groups.title: The sleepy lizard (Tiliqua rugosa)
groups.instruction: Complete the notes. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

transcript.text: Last week, we started looking at reptiles, including crocodiles and snakes.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Today, I’d like us to have a look at another reptile – the lizard – and in particular, at some studies that have been done on a particular type of lizard whose Latin name istiliqua rugosa.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This is commonly known as the sleepy lizard, because it’s quite slow in its movements and spends quite a lot of its time dozing under rocks or lying in the sun.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: I’ll start with a general description.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Sleepy lizards live in Western and South Australia, where they’re quite common.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Unlike European lizards, which are mostly small, green and fast-moving, sleepy lizards are brown, but what’s particularly distinctive about them is the colour of their tongue, which is dark blue, in contrast with the lining of their mouth which is bright pink.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And they’re much bigger than most European lizards.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: They have quite a varied diet, including insects and even small animals, but they mostly eat plants of varying kinds.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Even though they’re quite large and powerful, with strong jaws that can crush beetles and snail shells, they still have quite a few predators.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Large birds like cassowaries were one of the main ones in the past, but nowadays they’re more likely to be caught and killed by snakes.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Actually, another threat to their survival isn’t a predator at all, but is man-made – quite a large number of sleepy lizards are killed by cars when they’re trying to cross highways.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: One study carried out by Michael Freake at Flinders University investigated the methods of navigation of these lizards.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Though they move slowly, they can travel quite long distances.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And he found that even if they were taken some distance away from their home territory, they could usually find their way back home as long as they could see the sky – they didn’t need any other landmarks on the ground.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Observations of these lizards in the wild have also revealed that their mating habits are quite unusual.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Unlike most animals, it seems that they’re relatively monogamous, returning to the same partner year after year.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And the male and female also stay together for a long time, both before and after the birth of their young.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: It’s quite interesting to think about the possible reasons for this.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: It could be that it’s to do with protecting their young – you’d expect them to have a much better chance of survival if they have both parents around.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But in fact observers have noted that once the babies have hatched out of their eggs, they have hardly any contact with their parents.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: So, there’s not really any evidence to support that idea.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Another suggestion’s based on the observation that male lizards in monogamous relationships tend to be bigger and stronger than other males.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: So maybe the male lizards stay around so they can give the female lizards protection from other males.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But again, we’re not really sure.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Finally, I’d like to mention another study that involved collecting data by tracking the lizards.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: I was actually involved in this myself.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: So we caught some lizards in the wild and we developed a tiny GPS system that would allow us to track them, and we fixed this onto their tails.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Then we set the lizards free again, and we were able to track them for twelve days and gather data, not just about their location, but even about how many steps they took during this period.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: One surprising thing we discovered from this is that there were far fewer meetings between lizards than we expected – it seems that they were actually trying to avoid one another.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: So why would that be?
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Well, again we have no clear evidence, but one hypothesis is that male lizards can cause quite serious injuries to one another, so maybe this avoidance is a way of preventing this – of self-preservation, if you like.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But we need to collect a lot more data before we can be sure of any of this.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER
